purpose: A selective map of comparison designs discussed in the review, not a census, causal attribution or performance ranking.
blank_meaning: Not represented in this selected comparison; not evidence that the paper lacks the test or quantity.

rows.label: Hayat & Park (2024*)
rows.source_location: Table I; Sec. IV.A and Table II; preprint p.16, Fig. 11(a) inset, Fig. 11(b) at x/Y=0; p.17, Fig. 12; p.18, Fig. 13(a) inset, 13(b); Fig. 16 decomposes chordwise friction.
rows.selected_comparison: Equilibrium and non-equilibrium formulations in unswept/swept separation; signed stress decomposition.

figure_example.measure: Sign of mean chordwise skin friction in the separated region
figure_example.note: Null denotes within the graphical resolution of zero for the unswept equilibrium trace. Negative denotes a resolved negative interval. The displayed observations concern means.

rows.figure_source_location: Table I; Sec. IV.A and Table II; preprint p.16, Fig. 11(a) inset, Fig. 11(b) at x/Y=0; p.17, Fig. 12; p.18, Fig. 13(a) inset, 13(b); Fig. 16 decomposes chordwise friction.
rows.comparison_controls: Within a sweep, compare the three wall closures using CharLES, a constant-coefficient Vreman SGS, fine-grid results and common case DNS (Coleman et al.). Fine wall-parallel spacings are 0.00625Y, first normal spacing 0.0025Y; grid stretched in y. The coupled LES matching inputs need not coincide across closures. Across C0 to C35, imposed sweep, spanwise velocity, pressure-gradient history/response, bubble thickness and matching-point placement differ. The sweep contrast does not isolate a term of a wall equation. A matched fixed-input ablation of that term is absent.

rows.label: Bae & Koumoutsakos (2022)
rows.source_location: p.4, Fig. 3(a,b) and testing paragraph; pp.6–7 Methods, Eq. (9), p.7 Table 1.
rows.selected_comparison: Velocity/log-law representations, matching-height range and refinement, channel and developing boundary layer. Refinement also changes the sampling location.

figure_example.note: Training bounds are open. The two runs share the friction Reynolds number and differ in wall-normal grid spacing and sampling height.

rows.figure_source_location: p.4, Fig. 3(a,b) and testing paragraph; pp.6–7 Methods, Eq. (9), p.7 Table 1.
rows.comparison_controls: Velocity-based wall model (VWM) and log-law-state model (LLWM) trained in constant-mass-flow channels at Re_tau about 2000, 4200 and 8000. Test channels use a prescribed pressure gradient and viscosity augmentation, which constrains mean total wall force in a stationary balance; a reported policy-output error does not thereby validate an independently predicted global force. At fixed Re_tau=50,000 the paired runs keep the learned policy, geometry, forcing, Delta x,z/delta=0.05; Delta y/delta changes from 0.05 to 0.01 while h_m^+ changes from 5000 to 1000. At 20,000 the analogous pair changes from 0.05/2000 to 0.025/1000. LES input field, numerical error and grid also change. No sole effect of matching height is identified.

rows.label: Lozano-Durán & Bae (2023)
rows.source_location: §§2.5, 4.1, 4.3; pp.A35-17–19, Fig. 9c,d; compare with the downstream textual summary on A35-18.
rows.selected_comparison: Building-block/equilibrium wall models with exact-for-mean and practical outer closures in the boundary layer. These are different numerical experiments.

figure_example.note: Each outer closure is paired with both wall models. The exact-for-mean closure supplies the intended mean input in a coupled calculation. Different closures define different error experiments.

rows.figure_source_location: §§2.5, 4.1, 4.3; pp.A35-17–19, Fig. 9c,d; compare with the downstream textual summary on A35-18.
rows.comparison_controls: Within an outer treatment compare building-block (BFWM) and equilibrium (EQWM) wall models while keeping configuration, Reynolds station, LES mesh and SGS prescription. Fig. 9c uses exact-for-the-mean forcing (ESGS) calibrated to mean reference profiles; Fig. 9d uses dynamic Smagorinsky (DSM) or Vreman (VREM). This is a common mean reference, not identical instantaneous inputs across six runs. Changing SGS alters resolved matching fields and feedback. The comparison reveals sensitivity of the coupled errors, and internal error conditional on the exact-for-mean treatment; subtracting them does not identify an additive physical fraction.

rows.source_location: Table 1 p.5, Table 2 p.6, Figs. 7–8 p.9 (Group 1), Fig. 13 p.12, Fig. 14 p.13 and Fig. 15 p.14 (Group 2, with Group 1 Neumann comparison in Fig. 15).
rows.selected_comparison: Outer-closure sensitivity of separation with reference mean wall traction imposed. Supplied traction is not coded as a predicted wall-stress quantity.

figure_example.quantity: Mean streamwise velocity at the first off-wall cell

rows.figure_source_location: Table 1 p.5, Table 2 p.6, Figs. 7–8 p.9 (Group 1), Fig. 13 p.12, Fig. 14 p.13 and Fig. 15 p.14 (Group 2, with Group 1 Neumann comparison in Fig. 15).
rows.comparison_controls: On the baseline isotropic Gaussian-bump mesh (Delta_c/L=4.76e-4; structured block 4200 x 176 x 168) and same velocity-Neumann condition supplied by the DNS, vary SGS among none, DSM, AMD, Vreman c=0.025, Vreman c=0.07 and MSM. Cross-mesh comparisons also change first-cell height. Group 2 holds a chosen SGS and mesh while changing between equilibrium and nonequilibrium DNS-conditioned effective-viscosity conditions. Fig. 15 compares those two with the prescribed velocity-Neumann result. The two effective viscosities are bounded below by zero and stresses are coupled to local conditions.

rows.label: Agrawal et al. (2024)
rows.source_location: Published §V, Eq. (17) pp.124603-11–13; Table I p.12, Fig. 6(a,b) p.13, Fig. 7 p.14 (Boeing). Published §VI, Table II p.19, Fig. 13(a–d) and Fig. 14 p.20, Fig. 15 p.21 (Bachalo–Johnson). The arXiv v1 plots are Figs. 4 and 10, respectively.
rows.selected_comparison: Equilibrium/non-equilibrium models, grids and speed-bump/transonic regimes; velocity and Reynolds shear-stress comparisons are distinct.
rows.figure_source_location: Published §V, Eq. (17) pp.124603-11–13; Table I p.12, Fig. 6(a,b) p.13, Fig. 7 p.14 (Boeing). Published §VI, Table II p.19, Fig. 13(a–d) and Fig. 14 p.20, Fig. 15 p.21 (Bachalo–Johnson). The arXiv v1 plots are Figs. 4 and 10, respectively.
rows.comparison_controls: Within the NASA/Boeing spanwise-periodic bump at Re_L=2×10^6, compare sensor-based wall closure (SWM) and equilibrium wall closure at each coarse/medium/fine mesh (3M, 12M, 52M cells), holding dynamic tensor-coefficient SGS, geometry and corresponding grid; EQWM comparator reproduced from Agrawal et al. [7]. First-cell-centroid matching means grid refinements also change physical matching height. Inlet is plug flow, diagnostics shared between closures, coupled matching velocity/pressure are allowed to change. Same solver properties alone do not fix freestream Mach. No numeric Boeing freestream Mach is specified in §V; do not assign the common quasi-DNS or another study’s Mach to this calculation. B–J has Re_c=2.76×10^6, a 60-degree axisymmetric sector and 31M cells in the main comparison; SGS, mesh and wall-model implementations stay fixed as Mach is varied within this geometry. Geometry, confinement, pressure gradients, Re and reference all differ between the two bump configurations.

rows.label: Dupuy et al. (2023)
rows.selected_comparison: Graph-model message-passing depth and law-of-the-wall baseline; integrated stress errors and reattachment are separate quantities. Depth changes information propagated in the model, not an isolated physical input intervention.

figure_example.measure: Streamwise reattachment distance divided by step height

digitisation.origin: top left, pixel centres at integer indices
digitisation.method: Read two trace centreline points straddling the downstream zero of streamwise wall stress. Interpolate x at zero stress, map the horizontal frame to [0,14] step heights and round to the nearest 0.1. These are approximate figure read-offs. The black reference curve is distinct from the dash-dot Le et al. comparison.

figure_example.note: N is the number of graph message-passing steps. The reference is the wall-resolved simulation. The three traces are a selected comparison. The study reports upstream reattachment for all its LES runs.

rows.comparison_controls: Step was outside the training data. Expansion 1.2, Re_h=5100, common 0.9M-point mesh, Sigma SGS, same mean inlet and upstream flow; wall-model changes confined to the bottom wall downstream of the step. Common reference is the study’s wall-resolved calculation. The law and GNN both align stress with first-cell tangential velocity and model its magnitude, limiting direction near reattachment. The coupled matching field and effective GNN footprint differ. N is the number of message-passing steps, so changing it changes the learned estimator and effective input region.

rows.source_location: Published pp.337–338, §7 mesh; p.338 Fig. 5(a,b), p.340 Fig. 7(a,b) and p.341 §7.2, Eqs. (12) and (29); source experiment by Buice and Eaton.

figure_example.note: Mesh size and treatment vary together. The interface offset is 5% of local diffuser height, and the recirculation region has an incorrect extent.

rows.figure_source_location: Published pp.337–338, §7 mesh; p.338 Fig. 5(a,b), p.340 Fig. 7(a,b) and p.341 §7.2, Eqs. (12) and (29); source experiment by Buice and Eaton.
rows.comparison_controls: Coupled 2D high-Re k–epsilon RANS, same inlet Re=18,000, geometry, 398 streamwise cells and experimental reference. Whole-configuration comparison: log-law scalable wall function on 30 equally spaced y cells across full cross-section (near-wall y+ 5–25); interface boundary conditions on 50 y cells covering central 90% (5% of local height excluded per wall; y+ 3–70), wall treatment/profile and normal mesh/interface change together. Low-Re k–omega SST reference calculation has its own 140-cell y mesh, max y+ 0.34. Authors checked grid doubling with an exception for y in log-law runs.
